stories.headline: Kamala Harris urges Dems to 'be ruthless' with power after midterms, demands Trump accountability
stories.note: Harris's "be ruthless" and Hillary's "post-Trump era" talk feeds the GOP case that Democrats want vengeance, not governing.
body: After Democrats took Congress in the 2026 midterms, former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and former President Bill Clinton all weighed in on how the party should use its new power.

Harris posted on X that Democrats must be "ruthless in using every lever of power" to deliver economic relief and hold President Donald Trump's administration accountable for what she called "deep-seated corruption." Hillary Clinton wrote that "The post-Trump era begins now," framing the win as a call for accountability and affordability.

Bill Clinton struck a softer note, saying Democrats have a chance to "rebuild trust" with humility and "an open hand, not a clenched fist" toward people who did not vote for their candidates. He also urged action on cost of living, health care, ending wars and tariffs that raise prices, and getting the national debt under control.
The White House and the Republican National Committee did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Why it matters: Harris's "be ruthless" line and Hillary Clinton's victory framing give Republicans a clear overreach message heading into divided government—that Democrats want retribution more than results.

stories.headline: Newsom breaks with socialists over billionaire tax as California voters appear poised to reject it
stories.note: Even deep-blue California looks ready to kill the DSA's billionaire wealth tax, a rebuke of socialist overreach.
body: California's Proposition 40, a one-time 5% wealth tax on roughly 250 billionaires that the Democratic Socialists of America backed, appeared headed for defeat as of Wednesday afternoon, according to the secretary of state's results.

The measure would have taxed assets such as businesses, securities, art, and intellectual property, and was written to apply retroactively to billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026. DSA materials said the tax would hit people who together own about $2 trillion and help cover a projected Medi-Cal shortfall.

Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the measure, telling Fox News Digital that firefighters, teachers, Planned Parenthood, and most of labor opposed it, and calling it a "badly written" one-time state tax that was already pushing people to leave. He backed a countermeasure, Proposition 42, that would block new personal-property taxes and certain retroactive taxes and looked likely to pass.

Economist Richard Stern of Advancing American Freedom argued the left misunderstands wealth as cash sitting idle rather than factories, warehouses, and machinery. Newsom said a similar tax at the federal level would be a "very different conversation."

Why it matters: Even in deep-blue California, voters look ready to reject a DSA-backed wealth tax while Newsom breaks with the socialists—a ready talking point that socialist economics fails the affordability test with ordinary voters.

stories.headline: DSA accused of ‘elevating’ antisemitic, pro-terror rhetoric after Hasan Piker hosts election stream
stories.note: ADL's Greenblatt says the DSA elevated antisemitism by putting Hasan Piker on its official election livestream.
body: The Democratic Socialists of America chose Twitch streamer Hasan Piker to host its official election-night livestream. ADL CEO Jonathan Greenblatt blasted the choice, saying Piker "proudly expresses support for terrorist organizations and traffics in antisemitism" and that the DSA is elevating that rhetoric, not distancing from it.

DSA-backed or supported winners Tuesday included Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Melat Kiros in Colorado, Donavan McKinney in Michigan, and Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York. The ADL has criticized Piker for remarks it says echo classic antisemitic tropes, including past comments about Orthodox Jews and Zionism.

Piker replied to Greenblatt with a vulgar personal attack and celebrated what he called a "blue-clear apocalypse," telling viewers "Trumpism is dying" and imagining Trump in prison. He had campaigned with Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who later limited joint events after critics accused Piker of suggesting Jewish Americans' support for Israel could invite violence against them.
El-Sayed said Americans should advocate without fear of violence and that antisemitism "is a scourge," without an outright condemnation of Piker's earlier comments.
Why it matters: Tying the DSA's midterm wins to a streamer the ADL calls antisemitic hands Republicans a sharp culture-and-security contrast as socialists gain clout inside the Democratic coalition.

stories.headline: DSA leader dismisses $49T cost estimate for socialist policies as a 'made-up number'
stories.note: DSA's co-chair waved off a $49 trillion White House price tag and wouldn't give her own number—ammo for the GOP affordability fight.
body: DSA national co-chair Megan Romer went on Fox News's "The Story" after DSA-backed candidates made midterm gains and was pressed on the cost of the group's agenda. The White House Council of Economic Advisers has estimated DSA proposals—including Medicare for All and student debt cancellation—at about $49 trillion, or roughly $355,000 per household over a decade.

Romer called that figure "outrageous" and a "made-up number," saying the White House "managed to come up with some math that made us look bad." When Martha MacCallum asked for her own estimate, Romer refused, saying the cost "depends" and "I'm not going to give you a solid number."

She argued military spending should be redirected toward DSA priorities such as amnesty for illegal immigrants and abolishing the Senate. MacCallum noted the defense budget is about $961 billion versus an estimated $47 trillion tied to DSA health-care ideas alone.
In a July Fox interview, Romer had stood by abolishing the Senate, replacing the presidency and Supreme Court, eradicating ICE, and abolishing borders.
Why it matters: A socialist leader who can't—or won't—price her platform while DSA wins seats gives Republicans a concrete affordability argument for the next two years.

stories.headline: Majority Leader Thune says Senate GOP won't 'stand idly by' as Democrats take control of Congress
stories.note: Thune says Senate Republicans will team with Trump to stop "Democrat extremism" even from the minority.
body: After Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said Senate Republicans will work with President Donald Trump to block "Democrat extremism" once the GOP becomes the minority in the 120th Congress.

In an X post, Thune credited the last two years with safer streets, more money in Americans' pockets, stopping what he called the largest tax hike in American history, securing the border, confirming Trump's Cabinet quickly, and seating conservative judges at a pace not seen since Reagan.

"As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we've done," Thune wrote. "Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we'll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism."
Available results so far point to Republicans holding about 44 Senate seats next Congress, with Mississippi and Alaska still unresolved.
Why it matters: Thune is drawing a clear minority-era line—Trump's veto and Senate Republican obstruction against a socialist-leaning Democratic agenda—before the new Congress even starts.

stories.headline: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker gloats over Dem blowout, promises jail for conservative enemies
stories.note: A streamer tied to Dem wins gloated about jailing conservatives, handing Republicans a ready overreach clip.
body: Hasan Piker, the progressive Twitch streamer closely tied to Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, spent election night threatening jail for conservative critics even though he has no power to jail anyone. Replying to commentator Matt Van Swol, he posted that conservatives would go to jail and everyone should "GET MORE WOKE RIGHT NOW," and he later told Laura Loomer she was "GOING TO JAIL."

Piker had campaigned with El-Sayed in Michigan and appeared late in the cycle with Rep. Ilhan Omar in Minneapolis. El-Sayed repeatedly declined to condemn him, saying the race was not about a "streamer from California," even as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called some of Piker's comments about Jews "dangerous and antisemitic."
Piker also celebrated James Talarico's Texas Senate win by amplifying Talarico's past "God is nonbinary" line and declaring "WOKE IS SO BACK," while urging the party to get "more socialist."
Democrats flipped both chambers Tuesday; early tallies showed about 54 Senate seats and at least 228 House seats, with more races still counting.

Why it matters: A Dem-adjacent streamer's jail threats and "woke is back" gloating after the blue wave give Republicans vivid overreach clips for voters who wanted affordability, not revenge politics.

stories.headline: White House official details what gets Trump’s attention in intelligence briefings
stories.note: Trump's cartel crackdown stays focused on seizures and victims—an administration win while Congress flips.
body: In an exclusive with Fox News Digital, a White House official said President Donald Trump's intelligence briefings on cartels often pivot from big networks to a single American crime victim, with Trump pressing what more the government can do to protect everyday people.

The official said Trump sees photos of drug seizures and quickly asks what else can stop the flow. The Homeland Security Task Force model ties together more than 20 federal agencies; White House figures for fiscal 2026 include nearly 12,000 arrests, about 161 metric tons of drugs seized, $482 million in criminal assets, nearly 13,000 weapons, and 676 criminal organizations disrupted.

Instead of racing to indict the same target separately, agencies now coordinate through a National Coordination Center so investigators hit transporters, distributors, and money launderers—not only kingpins. "Now we're all indicting together," the official said.

Examples cited include Trinitarios racketeering cases in Massachusetts, multi-defendant narcotics cases in Louisiana, and a May Justice Department sweep against Tren de Aragua spanning six districts. The official said the gang is "on their heels" under the concerted effort.

Why it matters: While Democrats celebrate Congress, the administration is still posting concrete cartel and fentanyl enforcement numbers—an executive-branch record Republicans can defend with Trump's veto pen.
